name: Bernard of Clairvaux
role: Cistercian abbot, papal adviser and crusade preacher (1090–1153)
summary: Bernard defended Christian kingship under divine authority and the Church’s direction of temporal power. He promoted crusading and austere religious reform while opposing attacks on Jews; his Wendish appeal remains disputed in its intended scope of violence.

decide-locally.rationale: Urges returning judicial matters to local authorities with better knowledge; specifically addresses church appeals.

more-religion-public.rationale: Urges the pope to pursue public evangelization and conversion vigorously.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Calls for the crusade to protect eastern Christians and the holy places; the statement's 'human rights' framing is anachronistic.

revolution-justified.rationale: Cites Romans 13 that resisting the higher power resists God's ordinance, and calls the Romans' republican revolt against Pope Eugenius ingratitude and sacrilege.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Royal letters affirm that a king can govern faithfully and justly.

political-violence-never.rationale: Explicitly legitimates killing enemies in properly motivated Christian warfare.

separate-church-state.rationale: Places temporal force within the Church’s two swords, exercised through soldiers and emperor.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Uses biblical authority to prescribe royal duties and the Church’s temporal jurisdiction.

self-interest-moral.rationale: In On Loving God, self-love is the first, carnal stage of love that must be restrained and turned to God and neighbour; charity seeks not its own.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Against Abelard, explicitly defends believing divine truths beyond rational demonstration.

population-transfer.rationale: Explicitly forbids driving Jews out, as well as persecution and killing.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Rebukes papal expenditure on wealthy crowds as diversion of resources belonging to the poor.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Defends episcopal hierarchy against arbitrary exemptions and unauthorized interference.

clerical-rule.rationale: In On Consideration both swords belong to the Church, the material one drawn for her at the emperor's hand and at the pope's bidding: clergy direct temporal power without wielding it themselves.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Letter XII protests royal interference with the bishop and threatens appeal to Rome.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Tells the Pope that making his will the law is unbecoming and that he should uphold earlier decrees and canons; rebukes King Louis for breaking agreements he had made. Both are rulers bound by their own and earlier laws and promises.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Demands that wealthy church leaders serve needy people rather than finance ostentatious display.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Protests Count Ralph's divorce on a plea of kinship, citing 'what God has joined let not man put asunder'.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Denounces luxurious knightly display, material vanity and covetous motives.

non-intervention.rationale: Urges overseas armed action to recover and protect Christian holy places.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Treats Christ’s earthly life and blood as grounds for restoring Christian possession of the Holy Land.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: His Wendish appeal demands ending pagan religion or the polity; scholars dispute whether its alternative means massacre or political subjugation.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Letter LXI explicitly grounds royal authority and obedience in divine appointment.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Defends the religious military vocation and urges knights to fight.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Charges Abelard with a new gospel and a new faith beyond what the Church received and asks the Pope to condemn it.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: He holds killing an evildoer in a just cause is no murder (In Praise of the New Knighthood), though he faults killing merely to save one's own life; he does not hold that killing is never right.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Describes the new knighthood as fighting bodily enemies and spiritual evil simultaneously.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Expects public rulers and soldiers to serve spiritual salvation alongside earthly responsibilities.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Frames crusading as protection, but authorizes campaigns abroad to recover sacred territory.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Commends an armed religious order alongside secular military authority.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Treats non-Christian worship as error to be reformed or destroyed (Wends) and asks that Christ be offered to all who have him not.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Seeks authoritative suppression of doctrinal error and treats papal orthodoxy as binding, rather than equally recognizing competing interpretations.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Writes that a command to do evil is not obedience but disobedience and that God is to be obeyed rather than men; said of commands of superiors in the monastery and Church, not of statutes generally.

notes:
Royal letters include a collective Cistercian appeal. Monastic common property is not treated as a proposal to collectivize society. Protecting Jews from violence did not imply equal legal status. No modern national martyr cult, universal interest ban, or specific apostasy penalty is inferred. The Wendish appeal is recorded at low confidence because interpretations differ. The source collection’s editorial commentary is not his speech. Remaining null statements reviewed across all ten themes; monastic asceticism and forest imagery do not establish modern environmental or technology policies.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 8 answers taken from it, 21 agreed, 2 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass from the Mabillon/Eales English translation of his letters and sermons, On Consideration and the New Knighthood (full text downloaded and searched by theme), not from the first audit's answers. Themes searched: economy (usury, property, charity, trade, tolls, labour), government (kings, the Roman republic, appeals, exemptions, elections), world (crusades, Jews, wars between Christian princes), society (marriage, heresy, poverty, dress), liberty, culture, ecology and technology. Economy, ecology, technology and most of culture are null: his letters and treatises do not speak to them. Answers on Church governance (bishops, exemptions) rest on his words about the Pope and the Roman curia. The Wendish letter's alternative of reforming the pagans' worship or destroying the nation is read as ambiguous; the crusade answers rest on his own appeals, not on what armies later did.
